title: Can a Catholic's or Protestant's other survey answers predict the beliefs on marriage, sexuality and devotion they were never asked, and do those associations hold for immigrants and across traditions?
lede: research programme: in GSS 1972–2024, a respondent's other answers predict an unasked belief or practice item at a median AUC 0.21 above the decade prior (Catholics: weekly Mass 0.86, premarital sex 0.85, same-sex marriage 0.88, abortion 0.75, divorce law 0.69); models trained on third-generation Catholics rank foreign-born Catholics almost as well but miss their levels by up to 11 points
summary: An open research programme on predicting (imputing) religious belief, teaching adherence, devotion and marriage outcomes from survey profiles, and on whether the learned associations transfer between Christian subcultures, decades, immigrant generations and, later, countries. Milestone 1 uses the GSS 1972–2024 cumulative file (NORC, release 3a; the split-ballot design leaves most items unasked at random). Across 49 tradition × item cells, weighted 5-fold cross-validated models given a respondent’s other answers beat the decade prior by a median 0.21 AUC, with lower log loss in 44 of 49. Among Catholics boosting reaches 0.86 for weekly Mass attendance, 0.85 for “sex before marriage always wrong”, 0.88 for opposing same-sex marriage, 0.75 for abortion and 0.69 for wanting divorce harder to get. Gradient boosting adds a median +0.003 AUC over logistic regression. A model fitted on third-plus-generation Catholics ranks foreign-born Catholics within 0.03 AUC on 12 of 13 items but misses their level by more than 5 points on 5 (certainty about God by 11), and a Catholic-trained model ranks Evangelical, Mainline and Black Protestants within about 0.01 AUC while under-predicting Evangelical sexual conservatism by up to 17 points: associations travel, levels do not. The GSS has too few Orthodox respondents (27–205 per item) to model. Milestone 3 ran both principled multiple-imputation baselines on 307 held-out Catholic item-years: chained equations (MICE) miss the year’s share by 4.7 points and the Si–Reiter Bayesian latent-class mixture (DPMPM) by 4.8, both worse than interpolating the neighbouring years (3.4), with Rubin intervals covering 82–83% at a nominal 95% and almost none of the same-sex-marriage years; a drift-aware conformal interval around a neighbour-anchored estimate reaches 95%. Adding the survey decade as one more variable in the mixture cuts its error to 3.55 points (paired −1.26) and same-sex marriage from 20 to 11.5, with Rubin coverage 92%: the missing period, not the imputer, was the barrier, though the period-aware mixture only matches the decade mean and does not beat interpolation. Limits: one fold seed, respondent bootstrap rather than design-based variance, shares not yet checked against NORC’s published tables, and global data (EVS/WVS/ISSP) awaits registration. It uses anonymised public survey data only and is not a tool for inferring a named person’s religion.
